Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Logan Riely/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NBA. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Rockets fans and fans across the country. This is to piggyback off of James’ post . Y’all know how I feel about KD. Great one-on-one scorer, horrible leader and teammate, negative locker room presence, and I’d rather have just about anyone else on my favorite team. Many of you are a little more nebulus on KD. Yet the fact remains, the team was no better and went no further with Durant in the lineup than they did without him. In addition, a recent report by ESPN’s Tim MacMahon cites Durant as the source of Houston’s obvious locker room issues last year. It was referred to as “turmoil”. Here’s what MacMahon said: “There were issues of connectivity in the Rockets’ locker room. [Fred] VanVleet directly and significantly impacts both of those issues,” said Tim MacMahon. “Kevin Durant was part of both of those problems. I would say you could even say Kevin Durant was at the top of the list of both of those problems. At the same time, KD was kind of thrust into — I’m not going to say unfair — but a position that didn’t play to his strengths, having to be the primary initiator down the stretch of games, having to be the default leader, the guy most responsible for the mood of the locker room. Those don’t play to his strengths. Those do play to Fred VanVleet’s strengths, and kind of take those burdens off of KD’s shoulders this year.” If things go south this season or even don’t improve, we all know KD could easily want out. He has a player options next season, so he could opt out and the Rockets lose him for nothing. In that scenario, they would need to trade him by this year’s deadline to avoid losing him for zilch. So what do you guys think? Do they trade KD at this year’s deadline? Sign up here to participate in the weekly emailed surveys: Cast your vote, tell us in the comments, and we’ll be back soon with the results.

stories.title: NBA Preview 2026-27: Reintroduction to the top 9 title contenders
stories.summary: Let's get reacclimated with the NBA's expected upper echelon by considering the cases for and against each team.
stories.detailText: Since we last experienced NBA basketball games that count, we have seen: 34 trades involving more than 90 players, including 11 All-Stars, plus a frankly ludicrous number of future draft picks; An estimated $2.5 billion in contracts signed in free agency ; 21 extensions of existing contracts totaling an additional $1.8 billion, headlined by Victor Wembanyama's five-year, $255 million not- quite -supermax ; The Los Angeles Clippers receiving the stiffest punishment in NBA history ; and The leading scorer in NBA history choosing to go to — and commute to — Philadelphia. That's a ton of business to sift through as we get set for the start of the 2026-27 NBA season, and try to do some back-of-the-envelope math on which teams we expect to find — and expect to find themselves — in championship contention come June. So, as I've done at the start of each of the last five seasons , with all of our hopes still high for the potential outcomes of all those just-signed deals and newly consummated trades, unsullied by high-velocity contact with the brick wall of reality: Let's get to siftin'. Join or create a Yahoo Fantasy Basketball league for the 2026-27 NBA season According to BetMGM , nine teams enter this season with championship odds of 25-to-1 (+2500) or better. Those nine teams feature 10 of the 15 members of last season's All-NBA teams … and they also feature major questions that must be answered between now and the postseason. Let's get reacclimated with the NBA's expected upper echelon by considering the cases for and against those top nine teams, beginning with a team looking to bounce back after falling short of a bid for a championship repeat: Thunder • Spurs • 76ers • Knicks • Celtics • Cavs • Raptors • Nuggets • Wolves (Mallory Bielecki/Yahoo Sports Illustration) Oklahoma City Thunder (+260) The case for: They have the league's two-time reigning Most Valuable Player in Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, which is a pretty good place to start. Also, they went the distance with Wemby and Co. in the Western Conference finals — a two-possession game in the final two minutes — despite their second- and third-best offensive creators, All-NBA wing Jalen Williams and breakout guard Ajay Mitchell, missing time with injuries over the course of the series. Those guys are back and healthy, which should help Oklahoma City maintain the effectiveness of a group that has finished in the top six in offensive efficiency three years running . Isaiah Hartenstein and Chet Holmgren return to backstop the NBA's best defense — a unit that allowed nine fewer points per 100 possessions than league average last season, which is the largest differential in 30 years, according to PBP Stats . The Thunder don't boast quite the same level of continuity that they had heading into last year, after trading away longtime point-of-attack linchpin Luguentz Dort, sharpshooting guard Isaiah Joe and reserve swingman Aaron Wiggins to chop down their luxury tax bill . But with All-Defensive selection Cason Wallace ready to step into an even larger role in Dort's stead, Mitchell joining Alex Caruso and Jared McCain in what's still a talented reserve corps in the backcourt, and a slew of other recent draftees looking to compete for minutes — including rookies Aday Mara and Bennett Stirtz, who've looked impressive in preseason action — the Thunder still have the potential to be one of the league's deepest teams. Oklahoma City finished with the West's No. 1 seed and the league's best net rating last season despite Gilgeous-Alexander, Williams, Hartenstein and Mitchell combining to miss 123 games. Get a slightly cleaner bill of health — for J-Dub, in particular — and some development from the youngsters, and the Thunder could very well push for a third straight 60-plus win campaign and a real shot at hoisting the Larry O'Brien Championship Trophy once again. The case against: As you might have heard, OKC struggles mightily with the Spurs , who beat the Thunder eight times in 12 tries last season and who don't appear to be going anywhere. Holmgren, in particular, seemed utterly bereft against Wembanyama in the Western finals; if he can't bounce back and find new answers to a particularly tall French problem that has plagued him since his prep days , the odds of Oklahoma City returning to the top of the mountain decline precipitously. It's also possible that the Thunder's posited depth proves more theoretical than practical. If losing Dort, Wiggins and Joe requires more minutes for Caruso (whom OKC has essentially kept on a regular-season pitch count since his arrival) and veteran mainstay Kenrich Williams, will the Thunder's bench drop off? Mara and Stirtz look strong in preseason, but how effectively will they — or former lottery picks Nikola Topić and Thomas Sorber — translate to live action if pressed into duty against the likes of the Spurs? I will grant that "can you get good minutes out of your ninth-through-14th guys" is the definition of a Champagne problem. When you've got championship expectations and you have to go through a monstrous opponent that has your number, though, all the pieces matter. San Antonio Spurs (+260) The case for: They return 98% of the postseason minutes from a team that finished in the top five in both offensive and defensive efficiency last season — one of just two NBA teams to do so, joining the Boston Celtics — and that went to the NBA Finals led by MVP finalist Wembanyama, who enters the season viewed by many as the ascendant best player in the world. The Spurs went 35-7 — a 69-win pace — from mid-January through the start of the playoffs . They were dominant through the first two rounds of the postseason, and outclassed the defending champion Thunder, beating them in Oklahoma City in Games 1 and 7. Yes, they came up short in the Finals, with the New York Knicks outscoring them by 26 points in fourth quarters , as they struggled with offensive execution and ball security, particularly in close-and-late situations. But they're already excellent, and the prospect of their most critical players — Wembanyama, Stephon Castle and rising sophomore Dylan Harper — actually getting better with another year of experience and development is downright frightening. (Ditto for forward Carter Bryant, a hyper-athletic defensive monster with the tools to carve out a bigger role in Year 2.) If the youngsters grow from their defeat, if De'Aaron Fox can play more like the steady set of hands that earned an All-Star nod than the injured-and-shaky version that disappointed in the Finals , and if incoming vet Tobias Harris can add another reliable two-way frontcourt presence alongside Sixth Man of the Year Keldon Johnson, the re-signed Julian Champagnie and Harrison Barnes, then San Antonio could have everything it needs to not only make another run at a ring, but finish the job this time. The case against: Progress isn't always linear. It's possible that, despite their arrows all seemingly trending straight up, Wembanyama, Castle, Harper and the rest of the Spurs' bright young things hit more developmental speed bumps this season than they did last year. Maybe leaning harder into three-guard alignments to more frequently feature Harper upsets the lineup balance that head coach Mitch Johnson found over the course of the Finals run. Maybe Fox struggles to get past his frustrating Finals, and the already loud rumblings over whether Harper should start in his place grow deafening. Or, y'know, maybe things go swimmingly, and the Spurs just find themselves on the short end of the stick this time against a Thunder team that projects as at least their equal. Getting to within arm's reach of the brass ring is hard; staying there is even harder. Philadelphia 76ers (+850) The case for: A team that won 45 games and made it to the second round of the playoffs added Jaylen Brown , an All-NBA two-way forward who finished sixth in MVP voting last season, and LeBron James, who was the best player on a team that won a Western Conference playoff series six months ago and who should be precisely the kind of connective playmaker who can help turn a talented roster into more than the sum of its parts. James and Brown join former MVP Joel Embiid, All-NBA point guard Tyrese Maxey and Rookie of the Year finalist VJ Edgecombe in a lineup that just might be the most talented starting five in the NBA. New arrivals Dean Wade, Kentavious Caldwell-Pope and Anfernee Simons bolster the second unit; first-round pick Labaron Philon Jr. adds some pop in the backcourt. New general manager Mike Gansey has given head coach Nick Nurse plenty of toys to play with as he works to improve on last season's 17th-place finishes in offensive and defensive efficiency , to build on the Sixers' first playoff series win in three years, and to wash away the bitter taste of their second-round sweep at the hands of the eventual champion Knicks. Philly has its fair share of questions to answer; it also has every reason to harbor real hopes about its chances of breaking through the second-round ceiling and, at long last, legitimately competing for a championship. The case against: It starts, as ever, with the health, availability and effectiveness of Embiid, who has played just 109 total regular-season and playoff games over the last three seasons. In that span, the Sixers have outscored opponents by 356 points with Embiid on the floor, and have been outscored by 729 points with him off it . Backup center Ariel Hukporti is already lost for the season ; Adem Bona brings energy and rim protection, but isn't a big-minutes answer in the middle for a team with serious ambitions; small-ball looks with Wade, Dominick Barlow and LeBron at center run the risk of getting overwhelmed on the glass. For the Sixers to get where they want to go, the notably slimmed down Embiid has to stay upright and ambulatory — and prove better equipped to defend in space than he was against New York in Round 2 — in a way that we simply haven't seen from him deep into springtime. Beyond Embiid, there's also the bit about the Sixers heavily relying on LeBron, who has played more minutes than anyone in NBA history and turns 42 in December, and skepticism in some quarters about how willingly and effectively Brown will operate in a context that will demand a dramatically reduced on-ball workload from what he enjoyed in Boston last season. If Nurse struggles to pull the right levers to get everyone their touches and put them all in position to succeed, the sheer talent on hand might not be enough to vault Philly to the top of the East, and ahead of their defending-champion rivals. Hey, speaking of whom: New York Knicks (+1000) The case for: ICYMI: They just won the NBA championship , and put together arguably the most dominant single postseason run the sport's ever seen in the process. New York returns the starting five that delivered the franchise's first championship in 53 years: Finals Most Valuable Player Jalen Brunson, the straw that stirs the drink ; center Karl-Anthony Towns, who played career-best ball on both ends of the floor during the title run; and top-flight wings OG Anunoby , Mikal Bridges and Josh Hart . Key bench guards Miles "Deuce" McBride, Landry Shamet, Jose Alvarado and Jordan Clarkson all return, too, while newcomer Andre Drummond gives head coach Mike Brown a veteran rebounding presence in the place of departed backup bigs Mitchell Robinson and Ariel Hukporti. The Knicks entered the postseason as a very good team: 53 wins, a top-five offense, a top-10 defense, NBA Cup champions, with an elite clutch scoring option in Brunson. Between Game 3 against Atlanta and the final buzzer of Game 5 against San Antonio, though, they became a truly great team — a harmonic convergence of a roster that produced more than the sum of its already estimable parts, capable of playing splendid and damn near seamless basketball . We've seen the Knicks lock into that rhythm and reach that rarefied air; we now know, beyond a shadow of a doubt, that they are capable of getting to that level. Who's to say they can't do it again? The case against: No team has Done It Again since 2018, and only three teams since the Shaq-Kobe-Phil-era Lakers' millennium-opening threepeat have successfully run it back: the Kobe-Pau Lakers (2009, 2010), the Big Three Heat (2012, 2013) and the KD Warriors (2017, 2018). Getting everything to go right once is hard enough; going through consecutive seasons without something significant going awry seems damn near impossible in the modern NBA, as Tom Haberstroh and I discussed this summer on The Big Number: It's not just that we haven't had a repeat titlist in eight years; no conference champion has even gotten back to the Finals after winning it all since the Warriors and Cavaliers renewed their annual unpleasantries from 2014 through 2018 (with the Warriors getting back in 2019, too). On one hand, maybe the Knicks' utter dominance in the postseason — two sweeps, a five-game Finals, no series going the distance — means they won't be bringing the same wear-and-tear into the title defense as their predecessors. On the other, they have worn their fair share of tread off the tires: All five members of New York's starting five have played at least 6,000 minutes over the past two seasons, a heavy enough workload to make you wonder whether fatigue could wind up being a factor for Brown's main players. Add in the potential significance of losing Robinson in free agency , the overall sour vibes surrounding the no-longer-ongoing negotiations on contract extensions for Towns, Hart and McBride , the way the East's depth and quality have risen around them, and the unavoidable challenge of going from the hunter to the hunted and having to face every opponent's best shot, and the Knicks enter ring night with their work cut out for them. Boston Celtics (+1400) The case for: Coming off four straight seasons in which they'd won at least 50 games with three trips to the conference finals, two NBA Finals berths and one championship, Boston seemed poised to take a step back. Jayson Tatum was on the shelf after rupturing his Achilles tendon in the playoffs against the Knicks. Jrue Holiday, Al Horford and Kristaps Porziņġis were all gone, dealt in service of resetting the financial ledger; head coach Joe Mazzulla would now have to see what he could make out of half a championship rotation and a slew of unproven contributors. What he made: a 56-win team that produced the NBA's second-best offense and fifth-best defense . Pretty good! This year's model will be different from its predecessor, of course, remade by the stunning trade that sent Brown to Philly and imported Paul George — who has made it clear he's not trying to replace Brown , but whose higher-volume, higher-accuracy 3-point shooting and higher-end off-ball defensive work might make him a cleaner fit into the overarching possession-game-winning superstructure that Mazzulla, Brad Stevens and Co. have built at TD Garden. Robinson comes in from the champs to fortify the frontcourt rotation alongside Neemias Queta. Mike Conley comes over from Minnesota to be the veteran sage in the room, bending the ears of ball-handlers Derrick White and the just-extended Payton Pritchard, young wings Baylor Scheierman, Hugo González and Jordan Walsh, and anyone else who might benefit from a little bit of hard-won wisdom at an opportune moment. The pieces seem to fit. And if Tatum — who played less than 750 total minutes last season after his remarkable late-season return from Achilles rehab — is all the way back to his perennial All-NBA form as he steps into the central role that Brown occupied last season, it's easy to envision the Celtics cranking out another 50-plus-win campaign and entering the playoffs unafraid of any opponent they'll have to face. The case against: Maybe Tatum, who missed the deciding Game 7 against the Sixers with left knee stiffness after his comeback, isn't all the way back to his perennial All-NBA form — or, at least, not enough to shoulder a superstar-level primary option workload. Maybe George, who has played more than 56 games just once in the past seven years, and Robinson, who has logged just over 2,200 minutes over the last three seasons amid various lower leg injuries and load-management plans, aren't on the floor enough to make the kind of possession-tilting impact that Stevens envisions. Maybe White, fresh off the worst shooting season of his career, can't iron out the kinks on his jumper. And maybe, as overwhelming a mathematical advantage as Mazzullaball grants the Celtics over the broader 82-game sample, the spring once again finds them between a rock and a hard place if the jumpers stop falling and Boston doesn't have quite enough of a point-producing Plan B. Cleveland Cavaliers (+2500) The case for: They bring back six of the nine guys who played at least 100 postseason minutes from a team that just made the Eastern Conference finals — the first time any Cavs team not featuring LeBron James has made it that far since 1992 — and swung a big trade that they hope will fill the hole they've had on the wing ever since their once and future King headed west to L.A. The Cavs went 21-9 after the franchise-shifting trade of Darius Garland for James Harden , fielding the NBA's No. 4 offense in that span and outscoring opponents by nearly seven points per 100 possessions that Harden shared with All-NBA guard Donovan Mitchell. Their backcourt playmaking, combined with the defensive acumen of Evan Mobley and Jarrett Allen, helped Cleveland grit its way through seven-game slugfests against the Toronto Raptors and Detroit Pistons to make it to a third-round showdown with the Knicks. If not for blowing a 22-point lead in the fourth quarter of Game 1 , a chin-check from which they never fully seemed to recover, they might've been the ones staring down Wemby in June. Alas. Rather than look to tear the foundation asunder after such a demoralizing defeat, the Cavs held firm: a massive extension for Mitchell , an attempt to reunite with LeBron, an eventual re-up for Harden , no mammoth tear-down swaps of Mobley or Allen. Instead, Cleveland shuffled the deck on the wing, taking part in a five-team, six-player, multi-pick sign-and-trade to land Peyton Watson, and subsequently sign the former Denver Nuggets swingman to a four-year, $88 million contract extension to man the 3 spot between their All-Star guards and bigs. (Also: Mario Hezonja's here!) It's a bet on Watson, who just turned 24, being able to both play a complementary role on both ends of the floor to plug Cleveland's gaps and eventually build on the strong stretch of scoring prowess he showed last season when the injury-plagued Nuggets put the ball in his hands and let him run with it. It's a bet that, with more reps together, the Mitchell-Harden partnership can reach an even higher ceiling, putting the Cavs in position to once again field a top-five-caliber offense. And it's a bet that, as ugly as that four-game sweep at the hands of the Knicks was, Cleveland's ongoing championship construction project — step by step, brick by brick, over the last half-decade — is closer to completion than its skeptics might think. The case against: There's a reason those skeptics keep arching their eyebrows — the sense that, no matter how good the Cavs can look during the regular season or for any discrete set of possessions in the course of the postseason, they lack the kind of cohesion and collective oomph that can get a team through its dark night of the soul. Maybe that's too facile an analysis. This team did survive Game 7 twice, after all, knocking out the No. 1 seed Pistons to advance to the third round, and the 6-foot-8 Watson provides the kind of length, athleticism and pop that Cleveland sorely lacked during the Knicks series. At this point, though, it doesn't seem wholly unreasonable to want to see this Cleveland core — Mitchell, Allen, Mobley and now Harden and Watson — prove that it can make it out of the East before you believe they've got the goods to do so. Toronto Raptors (+2500) The case for: The Raptors exited last season as a 46-win team with a top-seven defense and enough toughness and physicality to push the Cavs to Game 7 … but with an offense that too often profiled as rickety at best. Toronto ranked in the top-10 in half-court offensive efficiency during the regular season , but that dropped to 16th against opponents with top-10 point differentials ; the Raps' 95.3 points-per-100 half-court mark in the playoffs would have ranked 25th during the regular season. They were 15th in clutch offensive efficiency during the regular season, and their playoff mark would've ranked 26th during the regular season. They've finished 22nd or lower in the total share of their shots that come from 3-point range in each of the last five seasons ; they made just 123 pull-up 3s en masse last season, dead last in the NBA by 46 triples. All of which is to say: It's difficult to overstate just how perfectly Kawhi Leonard — who last season made 88 pull-up 3s by himself , led the NBA in points per touch , averaged a career-high 27.9 points per game on 51/39/89 shooting splits and was one of the most prolific fourth-quarter scorers in the league — fills the gaps in this team's résumé. Importing an All-NBA offense-unto-himself reduces the playmaking and shot-creation burden on every other Raptor, which should result in Scottie Barnes, Immanuel Quickley, RJ Barrett and Co. having more space to operate, cleaner looks to cash out, and easier opportunities than they saw in an often congested half-court attack. And slotting in Leonard — who finished top-15 in the league in steals and deflections last season — should only further fortify Darko Rajaković's pressure-packing defense; the prospect of trying to probe for openings in lineups featuring Leonard, Barnes, rising sophomore Collin Murray-Boyles, Ja'Kobe Walter and the just-extended Jamal Shead is enough to induce claustrophobia in opposing perimeter players. It's been understandably and justifiably obscured by the drama surrounding the investigation into salary-cap circumvention and his subsequent exit from L.A., but the version of Leonard we just saw was arguably one of the five or six best players in the entire NBA last season. If the Raptors get that version for 2,000 minutes — and, obviously and most crucially, get it into April, May and hopefully June — then this becomes a seriously dangerous outfit. The case against: If they don't get that version — and here's where we remind ourselves that Kawhi has played 65 games just twice in the last nine years, hasn't finished a postseason healthy since 2020, and hasn't played more than two postseason rounds since the Raptors' 2019 title — then all that stuff goes up in smoke. (More practically: If the Raptors wind up leaning into smaller-ball looks, with CMB replacing veteran Jakob Poeltl at the 5, will their rim protection and rebounding suffer against the best opponents? And even with Leonard stepping in for Brandon Ingram and Gradey Dick, is there still not quite enough shooting on this roster?) We're about three and a half years removed from a team trading a bunch of draft capital for a 34-year-old All-NBA forward with the expectation that it would help vault them into the upper reaches of contention; the Kevin Durant era in Phoenix didn't work out so hot. Maybe, due to the presence of Barnes and the picks they've still got access to, the Raptors are better positioned to weather such a disappointment without cratering. But getting Kawhi at a bargain price doesn't mean there's no downside risk of relying on him to get where you want to go. Denver Nuggets (+2500) The case for: They still have Nikola Jokić, and you still don't. Even with Jokić, Aaron Gordon, Christian Braun, Cameron Johnson and Peyton Watson combining to miss 129 games, Denver still fielded by far the NBA's No. 1 offense and won 54 games last season. The Nuggets annihilated opponents by 18.8 points-per-100 with Jokić, Murray and Gordon all on the floor last season; the framework of what's made this team work at such a high level for the better part of a decade is still here. Get healthier seasons from Gordon and Johnson, a bounce-back from Braun — who shot just 30.1% from 3-point range last season after knocking 'em down at a 38.4% clip over his first three years — and just a sprinkling of production from someone off the bench (DeMar DeRozan? Tyus Jones? Marvin Bagley?) and nobody's going to want to see this offense come springtime. The case against: They will , however, probably be excited to see a Denver defense that has finished 21st in points allowed per possession in each of the last two seasons . The Nuggets don't force turnovers, don't protect the rim and really don't stop opponents on the fast break; they've allowed more than 1.3 points per play in transition in each of the last two seasons, bottom-two marks in the league. If that doesn't improve dramatically, the Nuggets' chances of winning three playoff series — already complicated by the presence of Oklahoma City and San Antonio, and by the drip-by-drip defections of depth since their 2023 title run — are likely somewhere between slim and none. And if the 31-year-old Gordon, who has missed 77 games over the past two seasons and been hampered by recurring hamstring injuries in consecutive playoff runs, can't stay upright and on the floor, "slim" may have already left town. Minnesota Timberwolves (+2500) The case for: After making consecutive trips to the Western Conference finals, the Timberwolves took down the Nuggets and pushed the Spurs to six with Anthony Edwards hobbled, Ayo Dosunmu limited, Donte DiVincenzo sidelined and precious little point guard play to speak of. Well, they've got a point guard now. And he likes to go fast. The theory of the case: The arrival of LaMelo Ball to pair with Anthony Edwards cranks up the offensive variance in Minnesota to a senses-shattering degree, affording the Wolves the opportunity to explore new frontiers in pull-up 3-point shooting volume and geometry warping on offense. Force the defense to cover more ground and you open up more driving lanes and opportunities to feast on the inside. Hunt early offense with LaMelo's penchant for hit-aheads and half-court lobs to the likes of Edwards, Jaden McDaniels and newcomer Jonathan Kuminga, and a Minnesota offense that has largely lagged behind its elite Rudy Gobert-helmed defense might finally catch up — a stylistic pivot that could make the Wolves considerably more formidable, and give them a hell of a puncher's chance, against Oklahoma City and San Antonio in a best-of-seven. The case against: It starts, as these so often do, with health. Ball played 72 games and 2,017 minutes last season, recurring ankle issues led him to average 35 appearances and 1,161 minutes over the previous three; if he can't stay healthy, he can't supercharge the offense in the ways Tim Connelly and Co. are hoping. It remains to be seen how effectively head coach Chris Finch can maintain an elite defense around Ball. And how comfortably LaMelo can shoulder the quantum leap in operational duties required of the primary ball-handler and table-setter of a team that harbors legitimate championship aspirations. And how neatly Kuminga, once again singing for his supper after taking a bargain-bin deal on a team that likely needs him to fit in (read: defense, rebounding, screening, running the floor) more than stand out (read: hunt isos, try to score 20). And how the defense holds up when the 34-year-old Gobert — quietly one of the most interesting potential free agents in the league right now — takes a rest. And how a second unit that's now heavily dependent on both Dosunmu maintaining his level of play and leaps from second-year center Joan Beringer and Terrence Shannon Jr. holds up against the best of the best. That's a lot of questions. They're different ones, though — and, for a team looking to zag in pursuit of a new angle of attack against the conference's top flight, maybe that's enough for now. Honorable mentions Hey, here's a fun fact: I've written this column five times, and each year, at least one eventual NBA Finals participant was not included in it! Last year , the Spurs didn't make the cut. The year before that , the Indiana Pacers didn't. The 2023 edition didn't include the Dallas Mavericks. The 2022 version didn't feature either the Nuggets or Miami Heat. And the first go-round, back in 2021 , didn't have the Celtics on it. Which is to say: We're almost guaranteed to see someone that you didn't just read about playing for the Larry O'B come June! (That's how probability works, right?) The teams that didn't come in under +2500, but that bear monitoring in the big picture, include: Detroit Pistons (+3000): Yes, the Jalen Duren drama was taxing, and yes, I have my questions about the net outcome of effectively swapping Tobias Harris for John Collins. But the Pistons added shooting (Collins, Isaiah Joe, Taurean Prince) to the core of a team that won 60 games, finished with the East's No. 1 seed, came within one game of the Eastern Conference finals, and absolutely hammered the eventual champion Knicks during the regular season with Cade Cunningham at the controls. Maybe we shouldn't be too quick to overlook them? Miami Heat (+3000): Hey, remember these guys? They finished above .500 and just outside the top 10 on both ends of the floor last season, and they just traded for Giannis Antetokounmpo — one of the few players who can at any given point lay legitimate claim to being the best player on the planet. If he's able to play closer to 70 games than the 36 he managed last season, and if Erik Spoelstra's able to find the right balance between bully-ball and pace-and-space lineup combinations, the Giannis-Bam Adebayo partnership could be lethal . Los Angeles Lakers (+3500): The last time Luka Dončić had a properly built team around him — screen-and-dive rim-protecting center, high-efficiency secondary scorers and playmakers, active 3-and-D wings — he went to the NBA Finals . Now he's got Walker Kessler, Austin Reaves, Quentin Grimes, Matisse Thybulle, Ziaire Williams and Collin Sexton. Maybe that's not enough to put the fear of God into OKC and San Antonio. But maybe it is. Indiana Pacers (+4000): The last time we saw Tyrese Haliburton healthy, he had the Thunder on the ropes in Game 7 in their own gym. I can't blame anyone who wants to pump the brakes on the Pacers getting back to that level. But I also don't have too hard a time seeing Indiana — now with Ivica Zubac to join the rest of that Finals core — hitting the gas to return to what it views as its rightful perch. Houston Rockets (+5000): A 52-win team that finished top-seven on both ends of the floor gets back the organizing-principle point guard (Fred VanVleet) that it missed for all of last season and the goliath offensive-rebounding center (Steven Adams) who helped form its ground-and-pound point-scoring identity, and adds a tough-as-nails veteran defender (Marcus Smart) who should be a perfect fit for the postseason pressure cooker. Oh, and they still have Kevin Durant, who just averaged 26 a night on 52/41/87 shooting, and a handful of 25-and-under dudes — Alperen Şengün, Amen Thompson, Jabari Smith Jr., Reed Sheppard, Tari Eason — who all still have the potential to take another step forward in their development. This team's floor is really high; if a couple of things break right, its ceiling could be championship-caliber.

stories.title: Tyrese Maxey is built for this
stories.summary: Much attention and scrutiny comes with LeBron James. It doesn’t bother Tyrese Maxey one bit.
stories.detailText: CAMDEN, NEW JERSEY - SEPTEMBER 28: Tyrese Maxey #0 of the Philadelphia 76ers poses for a portrait during media day at the Philadelphia 76ers Training Complex on September 28, 2026 in Camden, New Jersey. (Photo by Emilee Chinn/Getty Images) | Getty Images The way the Sixers’ practice facility in Camden is designed, the media only gets to interact with players on the practice floor — by design, of course. The players have their own parking lot (with a roof for their super nice cars) and entrance on the far end of the building. The media members park amongst the regular people outside the facility gates and our exit is on the opposite end of the building. So, you could imagine my surprise when I encountered Tyrese Maxey walking out in the same direction I was. “You lost?” I asked. “Nah, I’m getting on LeBron’s helicopter,” Maxey said with a laugh. He proceeded to walk out of the gated space, awaiting a ride. As I drove away, there was Maxey, an All-NBA performer on a max contract, sitting on the curb, waiting for a ride. It was quite the dichotomy after seeing James take off from managing partner Josh Harris’ helipad atop the franchise’s business building. “One of us left on the helicopter,” Maxey said, “the other one sitting on the curb.” Helicopter or not, James has acknowledged not every organization and player can handle what comes with rostering arguably the greatest player of all time. We’ve already gotten small tastes of it, with a recent notable example over the whole rumored (and debunked) LeBron-Joel Embiid situation . There’s attention. There’s scrutiny. It can absolutely become a circus. But there might not be a better player built for the current situation than Maxey. Think about all Maxey has been through since he was drafted in 2020. He missed the bulk of training camp that year because he got COVID. He had a weird rookie season. He was too good for Doc Rivers to leave on the bench, but the Hall of Fame coach’s reticence to play young players led to Maxey getting inconsistent minutes. He was also in trade rumors for James Harden and Kyle Lowry, both of whom would eventually become his teammates. He saw Ben Simmons hold out and his role increase with the ball in his hands more. He was here for the Harden trade and moved back into an off-ball role. And remember the next year when Rivers told everyone it was Maxey’s idea to come off the bench after returning from injury? Hilarious. Harden’s ensuing holdout vaulted Maxey to second in the pecking order, leading to his first All-Star appearance and the league’s Most Improved Player Award. With Tobias Harris and his exorbitant contract gone, Maxey was able to welcome Paul George aboard — and we all remember how 2024-25 went. It was a nightmare for Maxey, Joel Embiid, the Sixers and the entire Delaware Valley. He grew from it and had an outstanding 2025-26 campaign, culminating in his first All-NBA nod. This offseason he became a dad, without question the most important thing to happen to him, but the second-most important thing was nothing to sneeze at. Maxey successfully recruited James to join the Sixers to play alongside newcomer Jaylen Brown and a ridiculously star-studded starting five. James hasn’t stopped heaping praise on Maxey since he got here. Brown, too, has lauded Maxey for making a difficult transition much easier by welcoming him with open arms. Labaron Philon Jr. has frequently mentioned how much Maxey is helping the rookie’s assimilation to the NBA. Mike Gansey did a hell of a job assembling this roster, but Maxey’s fingerprints are all over it. It’s not hyperbolic to say Maxey has changed the entire trajectory of this organization. Imagine if he hadn’t become the player he is after being selected 21st overall. The Sixers would’ve likely been stuck in NBA purgatory. And if not for the positive culture he’s created in the locker room, this franchise could’ve gone sideways at multiple points over the last seven years. James has acknowledged it’s not always easy being his teammate. Not because of anything on the court, but with the scrutiny and attention that comes with a team he’s on. If any player can manage it, it’s Maxey. He was asked on media day what it’s like to be in this position, where he’s been LeBron James’ workout partner and now teammate. “What if I said LeBron was my workout partner?” he joked. Maxey was asked about the extra attention LeBron brings. “I wanted Bron, I didn’t want y’all,” he joked again. Then, he got serious. “Listen, with me, I’m focused on basketball, a job,” he said. “The rest of that, I’m not really worried about it. That doesn’t really bother me, honestly. I’ve been blessed to play in Philadelphia for my entire career so far. I played in Kentucky. I’m kind of used to the noise and all those different things, so that doesn’t bother me. “My biggest thing is I want to help my teammates, this organization, try to win basketball games and try to win at the highest level. So the rest of that, the hoopla, all that, all y’all people being here, that doesn’t bother me.” Holdouts, drama, injuries, mismanaged rosters, coaching malpractice, losing, media scrutiny, a fan base that expects nothing short of greatness — Maxey has handled it all. LeBron’s helicopter flying overhead while he sits on a curb is worth nothing more than a chuckle. “I ain’t gonna lie,” he said, “that was funny.“

stories.title: JJ Redick wants Walker Kessler to be relentless this season
stories.summary: Both Redick and Kessler believe plenty of success will come simply through playing hard
stories.detailText: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - OCTOBER 13: Yaxel Lendeborg #1 of the Golden State Warriors is fouled by Walker Kessler #14 of the Los Angeles Lakers in the second quarter of a preseason game at T-Mobile Arena on October 13, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Los Angeles Lakers are expecting big things of Walker Kessler this season. They love both his skill-set and how it fits alongside their star duo of Luka Dončić and Austin Reaves. It’s why they were willing to send a pair of first-round picks and first-round pick swaps to the Utah Jazz while inking Kessler to a four-year, $130 million deal this summer. To help achieve those big things, Kessler and Lakers head coach JJ Redick are latching onto a singular word, one they think should reverberate through Kessler’s approach all over the floor. “The word I’ve used with him, the challenge is just being relentless. Just in terms of the motor on both ends, running the floor, diving, screening, crashing the glass, playing off Luka and [Reaves],” Redick told reporters Tuesday after Kessler made his preseason debut. “He’s going to have opportunities to playmake in the pocket. That’s just the nature of how teams guard those two guys. His stats are going to naturally come just from playing hard. I thought he did a great job of that. Again, that’s like a very encouraging thing when you have multiple guys on the team that you feel like are going to do the little stuff that maybe doesn’t always show up in a box score, but helps the team.” Kessler left a positive impression to open his Lakers tenure, with 11 points (4-of-6 shooting), nine rebounds, one assist, one steal and one block Tuesday against the Golden State Warriors. He knows if he plays relentlessly, high-level impact should follow, so he intends to try and maximize every single possession, which will manifest in array of ways that benefit Los Angeles. “JJ and I talked and that’s kind of what we came up with this year is relentless,” Kessler said. “For me, that means just crashing every time, trying to be a presence in the paint, run, play hard, don’t take plays off on the offensive end, defensive end. So that’s going to be my goal for this year.” Kessler’s next opportunity to embody that relentless mantra comes Friday against the Denver Nuggets in the Lakers’ preseason finale before their regular season kicks off Oct. 21 at home facing the Warriors. stories.title: JJ Redick throws Lakers players under bus to excuse Bronny James’ poor play
stories.summary: Los Angeles Lakers coach JJ Redick defended Bronny James' preseason struggles with an eyebrow-raising excuse.
stories.detailText: Bronny James is eager to prove he can thrive in the NBA outside of father LeBron’s shadow this season. But he has looked exposed without his father so far in the Lakers’ preseason . Los Angeles Lakers guard Bronny James (9) looks on against the Sacramento Kings during a game at Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles, Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The 22-year-old went scoreless on two field-goal attempts, along with one rebound and four turnovers in 11 minutes against the Warriors on Tuesday night. Through four preseason games, James has averaged 2.8 points, 2.8 rebounds and 3.3 assists in 17.5 minutes per game. Lakers coach JJ Redick was asked how he assesses James’ “confidence and aggression” throughout this preseason, given how last season ended for him. “Yeah. I thought he had a really nice September and a good summer. I don’t think he has played well in the four preseason games, but he has had good practices,” Redick said. Los Angeles Lakers head coach JJ Redick speaks to Bronny James during the second half of a preseason game against the Golden State Warriors at Chase Center in San Francisco, California, Sunday, Oct. 6, 2026. Getty Images “Again, some of it is just rhythm; some of it is who he’s playing with. He’s playing a lot of minutes, especially in the second half of games, with our two-way guys. And tonight, he played with Rafael [Castro], who has been with us for three days,” he continued. “Some of it is the group he’s with; I think that is not necessarily setting him up for success,” Redick added. JJ Redick on Bronny: “I don’t think he’s played well in the four preseason games, but he’s had good practices… Some of it is like the group he’s with; I think that is not necessarily setting him up for success.” pic.twitter.com/6jEhPBhsSS — NBABase (@TheNBABase) October 14, 2026 Redick’s answer about James has gotten a lot of attention on social media, as many fans feel like he’s trying to excuse James’ poor play on the teammates he has been playing with . There might be some truth to James’ supporting cast doing him no favors. But those who are watching the Lakers this preseason can clearly see James is struggling, regardless of who he’s on the court with. stories.title: For Julius Randle, a chance at renewal and vindication in New York
stories.summary: After two years in Minneapolis, Julius Randle returns to New York.
stories.detailText: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - OCTOBER 06: Tidjane Salaun #31 of the Charlotte Hornets guards Julius Randle #30 of the Brooklyn Nets in the first half during their preseason game at Spectrum Center on October 06, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Jacob Kupferman/Getty Images) | Getty Images In Minneapolis on Monday night, Timberwolves coach Chris Finish made a veiled criticism that seemed to be directed at Julius Randle. He said that Minny had traded “moodiness for giddiness.” Although Finch didn’t name names, the general belief was he was talking about exchanging Randle (moodiness) for LaMelo Ball (giddiness.) "We've traded moodiness for giddiness." The Timberwolves come to NYC with their new backcourt of Anthony Edwards and LaMelo Ball. Wolves coach Chris Finch said Minny checked in with the Hornets on Ball a few times before they actually got him. While Ball and Edwards could be… pic.twitter.com/eOF1u6bUq4 — Mike Vorkunov (@MikeVorkunov) October 12, 2026 The two were not traded directly for one another. The Nets got Randle along with a late first for Nic Claxton and a high second in what was a salary dump just before the Draft. Then that deal was folded into a previously agreed trade that brought Ball over from Charlotte for Naz Reid and picks. And as Jon Krawczynski of The Athletic reported, two other players Naz Reid and Jaden McDaniels were also seen as moody and were also dispatched. Moreover, Finch had noted a week ago that he had mismanaged Randle’s role in the Minnesota offense. “That was on me,” he admitted. Still the message was clear … and controversial . Finch is happy with the exchange. Randle, who has yet to have an opportunity to respond, is happy too in Brooklyn. He’s said so more than once. Despite what others might think of his personality, Randle is a force to be reckoned with. As we’ve noted, over the past eight seasons, he’s averaged 21.7 points, 8.9 rebounds and played in an average of 68 games, including 79 last season. No NBA player can match that distinction. Moreover, during that span, the 31-year-old was voted Most Improved Player (2021), selected to the All-Star Game three times (2021, 2023, 2024) and was named All-NBA twice (2021 and 2023.) A big reason for the difference between Minnesota and Brooklyn is that the player and team need each other and his head coach here makes no excuses. Jordi Fernandez likes Julius Randle. “Yeah, absolutely. It’s incredible, man,” Randle told The Post about his reception in Brooklyn. “Everybody knows it’s a business and things happen. But when you’re somewhere where you’re really wanted, and you have that validation with an organization really appreciating you and what you bring to the table, it’s an incredible feeling. “It just drops the anxiety and just the worry or the pressure. You just feel like you can be your best self. So, from Day 1, I felt that: the support. I damn near get goose bumps just thinking about it, because the support has been amazing. I’m loving every part of it. I appreciate them just as much as they appreciate me.” Randle also told Brian Lewis that he believes he is in his prime, capable of a career year like the ones Fernandez has coaxed out of Dennis Schroder, Cam Johnson and of course he current teammate and frontcourt partner, Michael Porter Jr. “Yeah, I feel like I’m the best I’ve ever been in my career. I’m in a perfect situation to play my best under Jordi,” Randle said. “Accumulation of wisdom and continuing to improve every year, I’m at my best version of myself that I’ve been in my career, and I’m excited to be able to utilize that under Jordi and help this team.” Fernandez already sees just how he can take advantage of Randle’s game, particularly his passing ability. “I think that this could be [Julius’] best playmaking year,” Fernandez has said. “He’s proven that he’s a very efficient player at very different levels. Seasons with the Knicks when he shot eight-plus threes, seasons where he’s isolated more, been in the pick-and-roll more, [he’s shown] his ability to playmake. And you put all those things together, for me as a coach, being able to use somebody in many different ways, it makes my life easier. I think that he will make his teammates better.” Indeed, in the Nets win over the Wizards two nights ago, he racked up nine assists in the first half. “[Julius’] ability to throw the ball on time and on target to his teammates is unbelievable,” Fernandez said post-game, as Erik Slater wrote Wednesday. “Nine assists in one half of basketball is not something many players can do. I haven’t seen it many times in my life. I think the only one I’ve seen is Nikola [Jokic].” Fernandez doesn’t seem to be bothered by any perceived moodiness. The Kentucky product and Plano, Texas native is also just happy to be back in New York City. He didn’t want to be traded after beforc he was traded two years ago for Karl-Anthony Towns, he was a big piece for the Knicks. Prior to his arrival in 2019-20, the Knicks had not made the play-offs since 2012-13. He missed out on a ring but was a big part of the Manhattanites’ return to relevance. Now, he says, he wants to do it again in the Big Apple, this time across the river. “Sean [Marks] brought me here because of that, because it was time to win. So, that’s just what it is,” Randle said. “I’m not here to lose. I don’t think anybody’s here to lose this year. So, yeah. “We definitely want to be a team that goes out there and competes every single night. We’re playing to win. That’s as simple as I can put it. I don’t play to lose. … At this point in my career I’m playing to win and give ourselves a chance to win every single night, take the right steps every single day and see where that takes us.” And of course his pre-season comment to rookie Mikel Jones Jr. that the Nets will “shock the world” has been adopted as the team mantra. In his story on Finch’s comments, Kaczynski noted that one big issue for Randle in Minny was the constant rumors that he was on the block, specifically in proposals that would have brought Giannis Antetokounmpo to the T’Wolves. He told Lewis that was not the case. Instead, he said it was more the fatigue of 2,610 minutes —12th in the league — over 79 games and a late hand injury (two broken fingers) that was the big issue. “The trade stuff is always tough,” Randle said. “But it’s at a point in my career where I’m used to it. You know every year it’s going to be something or some type of rumor, so that really wasn’t it. More than anything for me, I tried to challenge myself last year, playing every game.” As for moodiness vs. giddiness debate, Randle will get his chance to respond to Finch on the court early in the season. The Nets will travel to Minneapolis on November 23. Julius Randle wanted — and needed — this trade to rebuilding Nets ($) – Brian Lewis – New York Post Nets’ Jordi Fernandez projects Julius Randle to make career-best improvement in key area – Erik Slater – Clutch Points Nets’ Julius Randle discusses joining team via trade this offseason – Shareef Phillips-Keaton – USA TODAY

stories.title: Pistons vs. Timberwolves preview: Getting a look at new-look T Wolves
stories.summary: The Pistons face the Timberwolves in a preseason matchup in Minnesota.
stories.detailText: Many people expected both the Pistons and Timberwolves’ rosters to look drastically different after ending their season at the same point in the Playoffs. Both teams are led by young stars in Cade Cunningham and Anthony Edwards that are still looking to break through to the NBA Finals. For the Pistons, the clock isn’t ticking as much with their young core locked in an Cunningham seemingly in support of everything going on. For the Timberwolves, rumblings have started about the possibility of Anthony Edwards trying to find a new team to play for, which means that the Timberwolves had to try to do something bold. They did just that with the acquisition of LaMelo Ball from the Charlotte Hornets. We now get our first look at the new-look Timberwolves even if we may not see their usual rotation for long since this is a preseason game. Game Vitals Where: Target Center in Minneapolis, MN When: Wednesday, October 14 at 8 pm EST Watch: My TV 20 (Scripps Sports Network) Odds: Timberwolves (-2.5) Analysis It is difficult to analyze a preseason basketball game given all the uncertainty around who will and won’t play and how long regular rotation players will play. There is also the whole other issue of players trying out new things they may not necessarily do in the regular season. The biggest point of intrigue for the Pistons is whether or not Jalen Duren will play. He sat out the first two preseason games as he gets reacclimated with the team after sitting out most of Training Camp over his contract negotiation. He is not necessarily in need of preseason given his status with the team, but it would probably be beneficial to at least play a few minutes in the preseason. Cade Cunningham sat last game, so he is another player that has uncertainty around whether or not they play. I would assume the Pistons want to get him on the court at least one more time, but could wait to do that until the final preseason game on Friday against the Raptors. If Jalen Duren and Cunningham do not play, I once again expect Daniss Jenkins and Paul Reed to get the start with a heavy dose of Ebuka Okorie and Tolu Smith off the bench. Both players had their moments in the overtime loss to the Washington Wizards on Saturday. Tolu Smith had a team-high 13 rebounds and Okorie led the Pistons in scoring with 14 points. Okorie has impressed with his ability to run the offense and although he may not get many opportunities to play early-on in the season, if he keeps up how he has been playing, it may force JB Bickerstaff’s hand to give him more minutes. For the Timberwolves, it appears we will at least get a short look at Anthony Edwards and LaMelo Ball together, as they have played in 3 of the 4 games for the Timberwolves during the preseason. However, the Timberwolves do have one more preseason game on Friday against the Bulls, so maybe they rest tonight and get in one final game on Friday. It is very strange that the Wolves will play 6 preseason games while the Pistons only have 4, but I guess the team does have some say in it and they may have wanted a few more to integrate some of the new additions. Hopefully this game doesn’t go to overtime for the Pistons. It took a last-second shot by Ebuka Okorie to seal the win against the Phoenix Suns in the first preseason game and prevent overtime and then the Pistons had the aforementioned overtime loss against the Wizards on Saturday. We shouldn’t have to be subjected to close games during the preseason. Whoever plays tonight, let’s hope for no injuries and hopefully no scuffle like the Pistons have had in both preseason games. Given some of the history between these two teams, I am not getting my hopes up. Lineups I am going to put down what I would expect the starting lineups to be if this were a regular season game, since there is no way to know who will or won’t play or what kind of experimenting either coach will do. Detroit Pistons (1-1) : Cade Cunningham, Duncan Robinson, Ausar Thompson, John Collins, Jalen Duren Minnesota Timberwolves (3-1): LaMelo Ball, Anthony Edwards, Jaden McDaniels, Jonathan Kuminga, Rudy Gobert Question of the Day Do you think we will see Jalen Duren play during the preseason?

stories.title: Can the Raptors Finish Top Four in the East?
stories.summary: Last year’s Toronto Raptors exceeded expectations, as the young and athletic squad racked up 46 wins, their most since the 2021-22 season, and finished fifth in the Eastern Conference before pushing the fourth-seed Cleveland Cavaliers to the brink in the first round of the playoffs. The Cavs’ second-half surge in Game…
stories.detailText: TORONTO, CANADA - JANUARY 11: Adem Bona #30 of the Philadelphia 76ers defends against Scottie Barnes #4 of the Toronto Raptors during second half of their NBA game at Scotiabank Arena on January 11, 2026 in Toronto, Ontario, Canada. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this Photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement (Photo by Cole Burston/Getty Images) | Getty Images Last year’s Toronto Raptors exceeded expectations, as the young and athletic squad racked up 46 wins, their most since the 2021-22 season, and finished fifth in the Eastern Conference before pushing the fourth-seed Cleveland Cavaliers to the brink in the first round of the playoffs. The Cavs’ second-half surge in Game 7 highlighted the importance of homecourt advantage (and experience) in the postseason. With the addition of former Finals MVP Kawhi Leonard, growth from the teams’ young core, and the scars of playoff battles, can the Raps win enough games to finish in the top four in a brutal Eastern Conference? Can the Raptors take the next step? Last year’s team was a pain for opponents to play against, especially in front of raucous Scotiabank Arena crowds. Toronto had a top-five defence that refused to let opponents get comfortable in their offensive sets, thanks to intense ball pressure from bulldogs like Scottie Barnes and Jamal Shead, but their offence was squarely in the middle of the pack (15th in offensive efficiency) and struggled to generate clean looks in the fourth quarters of tight games. Adding a two-way superstar like Kawhi should only bolster an already-strong defence, while adding a proven late-game scorer who can help get them unstuck in late-game situations. Still, though, a few question marks remain. TORONTO, ON- APRIL 12 – Guard Garrett Temple #17 of the Toronto Raptors greets guard Immanuel Quickley #5 of the Toronto Raptors during player introductions as the Toronto Raptors play the Brooklyn Nets at Scotiabank Arena in Toronto. April 12, 2026. Steve Russell/Toronto Star (Photo by Steve Russell/Toronto Star via Getty Images) | Toronto Star via Getty Images The ‘25-’26 Raptors were a below-average three-point shooting team, which restricted the spacing that Barnes, a slasher who thrives in transition, needs to dominate, and they were in the bottom half of the league in both offensive and defensive rebounding. Their ability to address those two weaknesses will go a long way toward helping them shoot further up the standings. The current squad is replete with quality guards and wings, but few are plus shooters. Leonard’s an excellent three-point shooter (38.7% last season and above 41% each of the three seasons before that), but he’s a medium-volume guy from deep. The big question isn’t so much whether or not he can space the floor for Scottie (he can), but how the spacing will look for Kawhi when he’s doing work in the midrange, which could be tricky given that neither of the team’s top two bigs (Jacob Poeltl and Collin Murray-Boyles) are threats from outside. They may go to some lineups late in games with no traditional big on the floor, perhaps with Barnes as the nominal centres, but they suffer on the glass when Poeltl is on the bench, given that CMB is on the smaller side and only averaged 4.4 defensive boards per 36 minutes last year. That might not hurt them against the league’s smaller teams, but giants like Karl Anthony-Towns and Joel Embiid, both in the Raptors’ division, can take advantage. On the plus side, better health from Immanuel Quickley and a potential mini-leap from Ja’Kobe Walter (40.9% from three last year), could offset their shooting deficiency and they have plenty of assets to pursue another big man should they feel they need one. Who else is in the race? The race for a top-four spot will be hotly contested, but the Raptors should be considered among the strong favorites. Kawhi has a long injury history, but suited up 65 times last season, and something similar should be plenty for a team that has plenty of depth on the wings, with Barnes and RJ Barrett both capable of scoring around 20 a night for a season. The East’s other contenders all have star-studded units but some concerns heading into the season. BROOKLYN, NY – OCTOBER 8: Tyrese Maxey #0 and LeBron James #23 of the Philadelphia 76ers talk during the game against the Brooklyn Nets on October 8, 2026 at Barclays Center in Brooklyn, New York. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this Photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Jesse D. Garrabrant/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images The Philadelphia 76ers vaulted themselves into the NBA title race with the acquisitions of LeBron James and Jaylen Brown, but even with those two and Tyrese Maxey and VJ Edgecombe in the starting lineup, Embiid is absolutely central to what they do, and he’s only averaging a paltry 32 games played over the last three campaigns. And on top of that, their backup centre, former Knick Ariel Hukporti tore his Achilles in the preseason opener, leaving them dangerously thin in the frontcourt. The Sixers may still be dangerous when the postseason comes around, but you should expect a fair amount of missed games from Bron and Embiid. It wouldn’t be shocking to see them outside of the top four when the season ends. Detroit felt like they overachieved with 60 wins last year, but John Collins could do a lot to help raise their offensive ceiling, especially if Cade Cunningham can help him look like he did back in Atlanta, where he scored 21.6 points per game on 58-40-80 shooting splits at just 22 years old. Few are as skilled at setting the table as Trae Young, but Cunningham draws a ton of defensive attention and there should be opportunities for him to feast. They might also get another year of improvement from an allegedly very disgruntled Jalen Duren. The Cleveland Cavaliers have been a strong regular season team as of late, and Peyton Watson is a nice addition, especially if he maintains his improvement as a shooter, but they’re asking for a lot out of a lead ballhandler who was born in the 80s , even if he was super efficient after landing in Cleveland last season. James Harden’s been healthy and available consistently, their all-offence backcourt could wear down as the season progresses. PHILADELPHIA, PA – OCTOBER 10: Tyrese Maxey #0 of the Philadelphia 76ers plays defense on Paul George #13 of the Boston Celtics on October 10, 2026 at the Wells Fargo Center in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this Photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Jesse D. Garrabrant/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images It feels like you can pencil in the Boston Celtics to win 50-plus games every season. Just as they managed to win 56 last year with Jayson Tatum missing most of the season, swapping Jaylen Brown for the older (but better-shooting) Paul George will likely do little to slow them down….if he can stay on the court. George hasn’t played 82 games in the last two years combined and rostering him instead of the consistently healthy Brown might be what drops them below 50 this season, but great depth and good coaching could keep them near the top regardless. The Knicks smacked their Eastern Conference foes en route to a historic NBA championship, but they were mostly fine in the regular season, looking discombobulated at points during a 53-win campaign. Star player Jalen Brunson is coming off of a surgery and head coach Mike Brown is unafraid to experiment with both the playbook and the rotation during the regular season, even if it costs them some regular season wins. Despite their playoff dominance, it’s unlikely they’ll go full throttle to chase the one-seed. Finishing somewhere around third again sounds about right for them, especially if some of their contract disputes lead to a shakeup, or even a distraction. Orlando has plenty of talent, but the Magic will be adjusting to a new head coach, while still dealing with a somewhat misshapen roster that has crashed and burned in the playoffs amidst a lack of shooting and creation. They should be in the playoff hunt again thanks to their defence, but likely not in the upper tier. Meanwhile, the Hawks (tied with the Raptors at 46 wins last year) added to their fearsome wing defence, but still lack a true offensive engine, despite strong production from Jalen Johnson and Nickeil Alexander-Walker. Charlotte is in a similar space without a true star, reorienting themselves after the departure of LaMelo Ball, and the Heat added major star power in Giannis Antetokounmpo but lack any real depth outside of him and 83-point scorer Bam Adebayo. As for the Washington Wizards, they are the Washington Wizards until proven otherwise. Prediction I think ultimately, the East will shake out something like this: Detroit Boston New York Toronto Cleveland Philly Atlanta Orlando Miami Charlotte

The road to the repeat begins now. stories.title: ESPN’s Brian Windhorst won’t stop banging the Cooper Flagg drum
stories.summary: Make sure you are on the ride and buckled in before the Cooper Flagg Express leaves the station.
stories.detailText: MACAU, CHINA - OCTOBER 11: Cooper Flagg #32 of Dallas Mavericks dunks during NBA China Games 2026 between Dallas Mavericks and Houston Rockets at The Venetian Arena on the Cotai Strip on October 11, 2026 in Macau, China. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this Photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Zhizhao Wu/Getty Images) | Getty Images The headline on Brian Windhorst’s latest column for ESPN reads: “ Why Cooper Flagg’s ascension is starting to feel inevitable .” In it, Windhorst argues that the NBA media ecosystem has been a little slow in recognizing Flagg’s ascension, stopping just short of declaring the second-year stud ready to “take the NBA by storm.” That he penned a column to that effect is notable, as Windy’s time is spent to a greater and greater degree behind a microphone or in front of a camera these days. He simply doesn’t write as many columns now, so Monday’s look is evidence that Windhorst thinks Flagg’s development and potential in year two is a particularly important story, league-wide. It makes sense. A lot of the big-name star power in the NBA has been shipped out east. The Mavericks as a franchise, remain, shovel in hand, digging their way out of a mountain of their own make, and are not particularly attractive to a national television audience as currently constructed. All this leads to a downward pressure on Flagg’s media attention. But Windy (and others, to be fair) stays beating the Cooper Flagg drum this preseason. ESPN Analyst Brian Windhorst is all in on Cooper Flagg. Welcome to The Resistance, Windy. | Screenshot from ESPN On Sept. 25, it was a segment on ESPN’s NBA Today, where Windy issued it glowingly and effusively : “I feel like there’s not enough hype around Cooper Flagg,” he said. “I know it’s hard to say because he was tracked at Duke very closely, but because Victor Wembanyama took that giant step forward last year, and really took the league by the throat, and because there was so much attention to the tanking teams going for the 2026 Draft, and the Mavericks themselves became one of the tanking teams at the end, I don’t think people realized how breathtaking Cooper Flagg’s performance was last season. He absolutely reminded me, on an almost nightly basis, of LeBron as a rookie. All the way back to the fact that LeBron was forced to play point guard as a rookie, and that kind of took him out of his game a little bit like it did with Cooper last year. The ability for someone of his size to play multi positions, to grab a rebound and then to go down and start the offense, to guard up and down the lineup, I mean, and really, his shot is way better than I thought it’d be. I think it’s going to keep developing, and I couldn’t be higher on Cooper Flagg. I really believe that he’s going to enter the top-10 of the best players in the league sooner rather than later, and that his trajectory is really right there alongside Victor Wembanyama’s in terms of the future of the NBA.” Brian Windhorst on Cooper Flagg: "In all honesty, I feel like there's not enough hype around Cooper Flagg. I don't think people realized how breathtaking Cooper Flagg's performance was last season. He absolutely reminded me on an almost nightly basis of LeBron as a rookie. I… pic.twitter.com/uf4cgqu3Sk — Oh No He Didn't (@ohnohedidnt24) September 25, 2026 The direct parallels with James, whom Windhorst built the early part of his career reporting on, and his rookie year, are startling. To think that Mavs fans could be watching the next LeBron in his ascendency is a beautiful thought to think. Just don’t let those thoughts wander into morbid reflection about how ownership might screw this one up. Then, on the team’s trip to Macau, China, Windy echoed his own sentiments, and if it’s even possible, amplified them in an interview with DLLS . “I am extraordinarily bullish on his future and I am really excited about his present,” Windy said. “Because of the dynamics of the league, because LeBron is in Philadelphia, and Giannis is in Miami and the Knicks are the champions, and the Celtics are the Celtics, and Wembanyama’s Wembanyama, and Luka is now separate from LeBron, the Mavericks are not on national TV that much. It’s a good and a bad thing. Number one, it means Cooper is not getting the attention he deserves. … Grab onto Cooper. Get in early. Be there, because the league is overlooking him a little bit right now. Again, it’s not like they’re looking at him and going, ‘Ehh, he’s not that good.’ There is a set of circumstances that is depressing him a little bit. Mistake. And look, at ESPN, we’re going to put LeBron and Luka on, you know? We’re going to put Giannis and we’re going to put Victor on. We’re going to put Durant on. We’re going to put Ant Edwards on, but I’m telling you, if Cooper was a stock, I would buy it all. That’s how I feel about him.” Brian Windhorst Says Cooper Flagg Is Being Overlooked pic.twitter.com/HE40B4yMwX — DLLS Mavs (@DLLS_Mavs) October 8, 2026 Windhorst isn’t the only one who’s comparing Flagg to James at this early juncture in his career. Flagg’s teammate Kyrie Irving did the same in some of his postgame comments after the Mavs’ second preseason game in Macao. “I give my respect to KD and Bron and they are on their own separate categories and trajectories and careers but I would say this, I think Coop falls in line in terms of having that competitive nature at a very young age,” Irving said . “He’s displaying in front of you guys what’s capable of and he’s only going to continue to get better.” "I give my respect to KD and Bron and they are on their own separate categories and trajectories and careers but I would say this, I think Coop falls in line in terms of having that competitive nature at a very young age… he's displaying in front of you guys what's capable of… https://t.co/JMoXET2V3S pic.twitter.com/uoNDZKiTDw — NBA (@NBA) October 11, 2026 It’s moments like these when I love being associated with this Little Fan Site That Could, because Windy, we outchea. We been here. We’ve been banging on the Cooper Flagg drum since jump. We made room for you, and we are here to declare that there is still room on the train for all of the lapsed Mavericks fans who had to take some time away from the team after the injustices suffered under the previous administration. Glory awaits. The team is the laundry, not the financiers behind the building the team plays in. It’s become clear before his 20th birthday that Flagg is not only generational, but an all-time great in the making. With a week to go before the Mavs’ first game of Flagg’s second year, it’s getting hard to contain the excitement surrounding the meteoric rise that this young man is about to embark on.

stories.title: Pablo Torre looking into LeBron James contract with 76ers: ‘Getting tips from NBA owners’
stories.summary: Pablo Torre is on the case.
stories.detailText: LeBron; Pablo Pablo Torre is on the case. During Front Office Sports’ “Tune In” summit in New York on Tuesday, the award-winning investigative journalist admitted he is planning to look into LeBron James’ use of a Fanatics helicopter while playing for the 76ers this season, a situation that has raised eyebrows to some in the NBA. “It’s something that I also have been watching,” said Torre, who broke the bombshell story about Kawhi Leonard’s Clippers contract and the team’s ties to Aspiration that led to a massive punishment for the franchise. “Of course, I know that Fanatics logo. I saw that. I was also a little mad that I didn’t get to get that one first. On that story specifically, I will say that we’re very interested and we are, of course, looking into all of the ways that is both a good story as well as something of interest to the league. And by the way, it may not be the latter, but it does appear to be the former as a business story.” Pablo Torre says NBA owners have contacted him about LeBron James flying in a Fanatics helicopter and he is "looking into" it. pic.twitter.com/8hdtkvFtzZ — Front Office Sports (@FOS) October 13, 2026 James, who signed a two-year $8 million contract with the 76ers in July, has moved to New York with his family since leaving Los Angeles in what was a booming free agency move. He has since opted not to drive to and from Philadelphia but rather fly in a Fanatics-branded helicopter, and James has been doing it throughout the offseason for practice and preseason games. “The deal we signed with Fanatics almost three years ago includes access to their corporate aviation,” a James spokesperson told Front Office Sports , which reported that James is allowed access to Fanatics Aviation as part of his contract with Rubin’s company. “It’s a feature in many of their deals with their largest athletes and we appreciate their partnership as LeBron splits his time between New York and Philadelphia.” Torre also revealed that he and his podcast, “Pablo Torre Finds Out,” have been receiving tips from NBA owners about the situation. “[The NBA owners] are like sending me your story and being like ‘What is this?’ because now I’m the guy who seems to be a lever on something like accountability even among billionaires, which is a fun plot twist,” he said. The helicopter commute is about 45 minutes, cutting down the travel time from what would usually be a 90-minute to two-hour drive. The four-time MVP took to the sky and returned to New York, landing at the VIP Heliport on West 30th Street. He could rack up roughly 67 round-trips between the 76ers’ 41 home games and roughly 26 home practices, the Philly Voice reported . James previously stated he plans to spend time between the two cities and would have “multiple residences.” The 76ers open the season against the Knicks on Oct. 20 at Madison Square Garden.

stories.detailText: Boston Celtics Last season: 58-26, lost to Philadelphia in first round of playoffs. COACH: Joe Mazzulla (5th season, 238-90). SEASON OPENER: Oct. 20 at Detroit. DEPARTURES: F Jaylen Brown , C Nikola Vucevic , F Anfernee Simons . ADDITIONS: F Paul George , C Mitchell Robinson , G Mike Conley Jr. What to expect It's a new era in Boston following the offseason trade of Brown to the Philadelphia 76ers . Only a few pieces remain from the core of the Celtics 2023-24 championship team. And there are lots of questions surrounding how this new version of the team will look without the homegrown tandem of Brown and Tatum that literally grew into the pillars of the franchise. Mazzulla has proven an ability to get the best out of what he has to work with, as evidenced in how the team played without Tatum last season as he recovered from rupturing his right Achilles tendon 17 months ago. But this may be the biggest test of Mazzulla's tenure as he looks to not only integrate new pieces, but make adjustments to an offense that has previously relied so heavily on 3-point shooting. Strengths and weaknesses The good: It starts with Tatum, who looks to be fully back to himself physically after rehabiliation from his surgery caused him to miss all but 16 regular season games and then Game 7 of their playoff loss to the 76ers because of a knee stiffness. George also enters the season healthy and at age 36 is poised to build off his strong playoff performance with the 76ers last season. Robinson’s presence brings an instant upgrade in rim protection, while also giving this group some great depth and options at center. Neemias Queta will likely remain the starter, but with plenty of support from both Robinson and Luka Garza . The not-so-good: Brown’s departure breaks up the dynamic between he and Tatum that worked so well for nine seasons and eventually netted Boston its 18th NBA title. George says he’s more than willing to yield to Tatum, but that will put the weight on Tatum’s shoulders to carry the team, a burden he hasn’t had to bear alone yet during his career. Players to watch Derrick White has tweaked the mechanics of his shot after a rough shooting year and will get more opportunities with Brown gone. Payton Pritchard started a career-high 50 games and average career bests in points (17.0), assists (5.2) and rebounds (3.9) last season coming off winning NBA Sixth Man of the Year honors in 2024-25. Last season also showed that he plays better coming off the bench, a role he’s expected to remain in barring injuries. Hugo Gonzalez also looks more skilled and comfortable at the NBA level as he prepares for Year 2. ------ See AP’s full NBA coverage here
